nodes.name: Computer System
nodes.note: A computer system combines processing, memory, storage, input/output, software and communication components to perform useful work.
nodes.hook: Trace one user action from input device to application result and back to the screen.

nodes.name: Hardware
nodes.note: Hardware provides the physical resources needed to process, store, move and present data.
nodes.hook: Classify each component by what resource it provides rather than by brand.

nodes.name: CPU
nodes.note: The CPU executes instructions and coordinates processing using control, arithmetic/logic and fast internal storage.
nodes.hook: Explain why clock speed alone does not describe total CPU performance.

nodes.name: Registers
nodes.note: Registers are very small, very fast storage locations used directly during instruction execution.
nodes.hook: Compare a register with RAM by capacity, speed and role.

nodes.name: CPU Cache
nodes.note: Cache keeps frequently or recently used data closer to the processor to reduce access delay.
nodes.hook: Explain why adding cache can help without changing the CPU instruction set.

nodes.name: RAM
nodes.note: RAM provides working memory for active programs and data and normally loses contents when power is removed.
nodes.hook: Explain why more RAM can improve multitasking but not necessarily CPU-bound work.

nodes.name: Secondary Storage
nodes.note: Secondary storage retains data persistently using technologies such as solid-state or magnetic storage.
nodes.hook: Compare SSD and HDD trade-offs for a college lab rather than a gaming advert.

nodes.name: Input & Output
nodes.note: Input devices provide data or control signals while output devices present results or cause effects.
nodes.hook: Classify a touchscreen and explain why it belongs in both categories.

nodes.name: System Buses & Interfaces
nodes.note: Buses and interfaces move data, addresses and control information between components.
nodes.hook: Explain why interface bandwidth can become a system bottleneck.

nodes.name: System Software
nodes.note: System software manages hardware resources and provides services used by applications.
nodes.hook: Trace what the operating system contributes when an application saves a file.

nodes.name: Operating System
nodes.note: The operating system manages processes, memory, files, devices, users and access to hardware resources.
nodes.hook: Separate application features from operating-system responsibilities.

nodes.name: Device Driver
nodes.note: A device driver allows the operating system to communicate with specific hardware using the correct interface and commands.
nodes.hook: Explain why installed hardware can still fail to work correctly without a suitable driver.

nodes.name: Process
nodes.note: A process is a running program instance with allocated memory, execution state and operating-system resources.
nodes.hook: Compare a program file on disk with that program as a running process.

nodes.name: File System
nodes.note: A file system organises persistent data into files, directories and metadata on storage devices.
nodes.hook: Explain why deleting a shortcut is not the same as deleting the file it points to.

nodes.name: Network Communication
nodes.note: Networks move data between devices through layered addressing, transport and application protocols.
nodes.hook: Trace a browser request from local network to remote server using each layer once.

nodes.name: Ethernet
nodes.note: Ethernet is a common wired local-network technology that moves frames between network interfaces.
nodes.hook: Explain what problem a MAC address solves on a local network.

nodes.name: Wi-Fi
nodes.note: Wi-Fi provides wireless local-network connectivity while sharing radio spectrum and access-point capacity.
nodes.hook: Explain why strong signal does not guarantee low latency or high throughput.

nodes.name: IP Addressing
nodes.note: IP addressing identifies network-layer endpoints and supports routing packets between networks.
nodes.hook: Separate local-link addressing from IP addressing in a home network.

nodes.name: Routing
nodes.note: Routing selects paths that move packets between networks toward their destination.
nodes.hook: Explain why internet latency can change even when your own computer stays the same.

nodes.name: TCP
nodes.note: TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream transport between applications, including retransmission and congestion control behaviour.
nodes.hook: Choose an application where correctness matters more than losing a little time.

nodes.name: UDP
nodes.note: UDP provides lightweight datagram transport without TCP-style reliability or ordering guarantees.
nodes.hook: Explain why a real-time game may prefer fresh state over retransmitting stale state.

nodes.name: DNS
nodes.note: DNS maps human-readable domain names to information such as IP addresses using a distributed naming system.
nodes.hook: Explain what still works by IP address if DNS fails and what becomes difficult.

nodes.name: TLS
nodes.note: TLS protects application traffic in transit by providing cryptographic confidentiality and integrity between endpoints.
nodes.hook: Explain what HTTPS adds beyond ordinary HTTP.

nodes.name: HTTP
nodes.note: HTTP is an application-layer request/response protocol used by clients and servers to exchange web resources and API data.
nodes.hook: Write a simple client request and server response using method, path and status code.

nodes.name: Latency
nodes.note: Latency measures delay; interactive applications are often more sensitive to delay and variation than to headline bandwidth.
nodes.hook: Explain why 1 Gbit/s internet can still feel bad in an online match.

nodes.name: Packet Loss
nodes.note: Packet loss occurs when transmitted packets do not reach the intended destination, forcing recovery or leaving missing state depending on protocol and application.
nodes.hook: Compare what packet loss looks like in a file download versus a real-time game.
